title: Proof
body_md:
Let $N_n$ be the number of open monotone paths of $n$ steps from $0$. Such a path is determined by its step lengths
$r_1,\dots,r_n\ge1$. It uses $n$ different bonds, which are open independently of each other, so it is open with
probability $p_{r_1}\cdots p_{r_n}$. The mean of $N_n$ is the sum of these probabilities over all the paths, and
the sum of the products factorizes:
\[
\mathbb{E} N_n=\sum_{r_1,\dots,r_n\ge1}p_{r_1}\cdots p_{r_n}=\Bigl(\sum_{r\ge1}p_r\Bigr)^n=[C\zeta(1+\sigma)]^n .
\]
Next we show that if the forward cluster of $0$ is infinite, then $N_n\ge1$ for every $n$. The expected number of
open bonds that have a given site as one of their two ends is $2\sum_rp_r<\infty$, so with probability one every
site has a finite number of such bonds. Let $A_k$ be the set of sites that can be reached from $0$ by an open
monotone path of exactly $k$ steps. Then $A_0=\{0\}$, and every site of $A_{k+1}$ is connected by an open bond to a
site of $A_k$. Hence, if $A_k$ is finite then $A_{k+1}$ is finite, and so all the sets $A_k$ are finite. The
forward cluster is the union of all the $A_k$. If it is infinite, it is not contained in the finite set
$A_0\cup\dots\cup A_{n-1}$, so there is an open monotone path of some $k\ge n$ steps, and its first $n$ steps are an
open monotone path of $n$ steps.

Finally, $\mathbb{P}(N_n\ge1)\le\mathbb{E} N_n$ by Markov's inequality. Together,
\[
\theta^{\rightarrow}(C)\;\le\;\mathbb{P}(N_n\ge1)\;\le\;\mathbb{E} N_n=[C\zeta(1+\sigma)]^n\qquad\text{for every }n .
\]
If $C\zeta(1+\sigma)<1$ the right-hand side tends to zero as $n\to\infty$, and therefore $\theta^{\rightarrow}(C)=0$.

For the unoriented model we count self-avoiding paths, whose steps can be to the right or to the left. A step of
length $r$, in either direction, is open with probability $p_r$, and dropping the restriction that the path is
self-avoiding can only increase the sum. The expected number of open self-avoiding paths of $n$ steps from $0$ is
therefore at most $\bigl(2\sum_{r\ge1}p_r\bigr)^n=[2C\zeta(1+\sigma)]^n$, and the same argument gives $\theta(C)=0$
if $2C\zeta(1+\sigma)<1$.

\label{cor:less1}
Let $0<\sigma<1$ and $\sigma/2<\alpha<\frac12$, and let $L\ge2$ be the smallest integer with
$L^{1-\sigma}\ge4\,W(\alpha)\,\alpha^2\zeta(1+2\alpha-\sigma)$. Then
\[
C_c(\sigma)\le1-\frac{1}{2\,W(\alpha)\,(L-1)}<1 .
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{(S1)} The binomial series is $(1-z)^\alpha=\sum_{r\ge0}\binom{\alpha}{r}(-z)^r$. Comparing the coefficients
of $z^r$ in \eqref{eq:gf},
\begin{align*}
\pi_\alpha(r)=(-1)^{r+1}\binom{\alpha}{r}&=(-1)^{r+1}\,\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)\cdots(\alpha-r+1)}{r!}\\[3pt]
&=\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)(2-\alpha)\cdots(r-1-\alpha)}{r!}
=\frac{\alpha}{r}\prod_{k=1}^{r-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{\alpha}{k}\Bigr).
\end{align*}
In the second line each of the $r-1$ negative factors $(\alpha-1),\dots,(\alpha-r+1)$ was multiplied by $-1$,
which cancels the sign $(-1)^{r+1}$. All $\pi_\alpha(r)$ are positive, and setting $z=1$ in \eqref{eq:gf} shows that
they sum to $1$.

\textbf{(S2)} We use $1-x\le e^{-x}$ in every factor of the product, and then $\sum_{k=1}^{r-1}1/k\ge\ln r$, which
follows by comparing the sum with the integral of $1/x$ from $1$ to $r$:
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{r-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{\alpha}{k}\Bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\alpha\sum_{k=1}^{r-1}\frac1k\Bigr)\le e^{-\alpha\ln r}=r^{-\alpha},
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad \pi_\alpha(r)\le\alpha\,r^{-1-\alpha}.
\]

\textbf{(S3)} To visit a site $x\ge1$ the path must arrive there by a last step, of some length $r$, from the site
$x-r$. Hence, for every step distribution $\pi$,
\[
u(x)=\sum_{r=1}^{x}\pi(r)\,u(x-r)\quad(x\ge1),\qquad u(0)=1 .
\]
Let $U(z)=\sum_{x\ge0}u(x)z^x$ and $\hat\pi(z)=\sum_{r\ge1}\pi(r)z^r$ be the generating functions. Multiplying
the last equation by $z^x=z^r\,z^{x-r}$ and summing over $x\ge1$, the left-hand side gives $U(z)-1$, and on the
right-hand side every pair $r\ge1$, $y=x-r\ge0$ appears exactly once:
\[
U(z)-1=\sum_{r\ge1}\pi(r)z^r\,\sum_{y\ge0}u(y)z^y=\hat\pi(z)\,U(z),\qquad\text{so that}\qquad U(z)=\frac{1}{1-\hat\pi(z)} .
\]
For Sibuya
steps $1-\hat\pi(z)=(1-z)^\alpha$ by \eqref{eq:gf}. Thus $U(z)=(1-z)^{-\alpha}$, and the binomial series gives
\[
u(x)=\frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)\cdots(\alpha+x-1)}{x!}=\frac{\Gamma(x+\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\,x!}\;\approx\;\frac{x^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
\quad\text{for large }x .
\]

\textbf{(S4)} Let $(a)_k=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1)$, with $(a)_0=1$. Gauss's summation theorem~\cite{dlmf} states that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss}
\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(a)_k\,(b)_k}{(c)_k\,k!}=\frac{\Gamma(c)\,\Gamma(c-a-b)}{\Gamma(c-a)\,\Gamma(c-b)}\qquad\text{for }c>a+b .
\end{equation}
By (S3), $u(x)=(\alpha)_x/x!$. Since $(1)_x=x!$, the sum $W$ is the case $a=b=\alpha$, $c=1$ of \eqref{eq:gauss}:
\[
W(\alpha)=\sum_{x\ge0}\Bigl(\frac{(\alpha)_x}{x!}\Bigr)^2=\frac{\Gamma(1-2\alpha)}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)^2}\qquad\text{for }0<\alpha<\tfrac12 .
\]
For $\alpha\ge\frac12$ the sum diverges, because $u(x)^2\approx x^{2\alpha-2}/\Gamma(\alpha)^2$. In the same way,
by (S1), $\pi_\alpha(r)=-(-\alpha)_r/r!$ for $r\ge1$, while $(-\alpha)_0/0!=1$. The case $a=b=-\alpha$, $c=1$ of
\eqref{eq:gauss} gives
\[
1+\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2=\sum_{r\ge0}\Bigl(\frac{(-\alpha)_r}{r!}\Bigr)^2=\frac{\Gamma(1+2\alpha)}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)^2},
\]
which is the second formula of \eqref{eq:Wsib}.

title: Proof
body_md:
We fix $\alpha$ in the window \eqref{eq:window} and apply theorem~\ref{thm:main} to $\pi=\pi_\alpha$. Since
$1/p_r=r^{1+\sigma}/C$,
\[
S=\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2\Bigl(\frac1{p_r}-1\Bigr)=\frac1C\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2\,r^{1+\sigma}-\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2 .
\]
The right-hand side of \eqref{eq:main} is positive when $S<1/W$, that is, when
\[
\frac1C\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2\,r^{1+\sigma}<\frac1W+\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
C>\frac{\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2\,r^{1+\sigma}}{\dfrac1W+\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2}.
\]
Hence $\theta^{\rightarrow}(C)>0$ for every $C$ above this ratio, and $C_c^{\rightarrow}$ is at most the ratio. Inserting \eqref{eq:Wsib}
gives the expression in \eqref{eq:CU} for each $\alpha$, and we may take the best $\alpha$. The condition
$\alpha>\sigma/2$ makes the numerator finite, by (S2), and $\alpha<\frac12$ makes $W$ finite.

For the closed form \eqref{eq:Ccf} we use (S2) in the numerator,
\[
\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2\,r^{1+\sigma}\le\alpha^2\sum_{r\ge1}r^{-2-2\alpha}\,r^{1+\sigma}
=\alpha^2\sum_{r\ge1}r^{-(1+2\alpha-\sigma)}=\alpha^2\,\zeta(1+2\alpha-\sigma).
\]
For \eqref{eq:simple} we choose $\alpha=\sigma$, which lies in the window when $\sigma<\frac12$, and drop the
nonnegative term $\Gamma(1+2\alpha)/\Gamma(1+\alpha)^2-1$ from the denominator, which only increases the ratio.
What remains is $\sigma^2\zeta(1+\sigma)\,W(\sigma)$. The expansion follows from
$\zeta(1+\sigma)=1/\sigma+\gamma_E+O(\sigma)$ and $\Gamma(1-2\sigma)/\Gamma(1-\sigma)^2=1+O(\sigma^2)$.

Finally, the lower bounds in \eqref{eq:asym} are those of proposition~\ref{prop:lower}, and the upper bounds follow
from \eqref{eq:order} and \eqref{eq:simple}:
$\zeta(1+\sigma)\,C_c^{\rightarrow}\le[\sigma\zeta(1+\sigma)]^2\,W(\sigma)=1+2\gamma_E\,\sigma+O(\sigma^2)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows the nine steps of section~\ref{sec:proof}, and we list only the changes.

\emph{Paths.} A random monotone path $0=X_0<X_1<\cdots$ is now a sequence of block indices. We call its first $n$
steps $\gamma_n$ open if (i) each of the $n+1$ blocks $B_{X_0},\dots,B_{X_n}$ is good, and (ii) each of these blocks
is linked to the next one. These events concern disjoint sets of bonds: the bonds inside different blocks, and the
bonds between different pairs of blocks. They are therefore independent, and
\[
P(\gamma_n)=g_L^{\,n+1}\prod_{k=1}^{n}p^{(L)}_{X_k-X_{k-1}} .
\]

\emph{Step 1.} $Z_n$ is defined as in \eqref{eq:Zn}, and $\mathbb{E} Z_n=1$. If $Z_n>0$, some block path of $n$ steps is
open. All the sites of its blocks then belong to one cluster. This cluster contains site $0$, which lies in $B_0$,
and it contains sites at distance at least $nL$.

\emph{Step 2} is unchanged.

\emph{Step 3.} Both paths are open when all blocks of the union are good and all links of the union are present. A
common block and a shared link are counted once. Dividing by $P(\gamma_n)P(\gamma'_n)$ leaves a factor $1/g_L$ for
every common block and a factor $1/p^{(L)}_r$ for every shared link of length $r$. All factors are at least $1$, so
\[
\mathbb{E} Z_n^2\le V_L:=\mathbb{E}_{\gamma,\gamma'}\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac{1}{g_L}\Bigr)^{N}\prod_{\text{shared links}}\frac{1}{p^{(L)}_r}\Bigr],
\]
where $N$ is the number of common blocks of the two infinite paths, block $0$ included.

\emph{Step 4} gives $\theta(C)\ge1/V_L$.

\emph{Steps 5 to 7} concern only the two random paths, so they hold with `block' in place of `site'. In particular
$\rho=1-1/W$.

\emph{Step 8.} The mean weight of a segment is now $m_L=\rho+S_L$, with
$S_L=\sum_{r}\pi(r)^2\bigl(1/p^{(L)}_r-1\bigr)$. Pairs of paths with $k$ segments have $k+1$ common blocks, hence
\[
V_L=\sum_{k\ge0}\Bigl(\frac1{g_L}\Bigr)^{k+1}m_L^{\,k}\,(1-\rho)=\frac{1-\rho}{g_L-m_L}\qquad\text{if }m_L<g_L .
\]
With $1-\rho=1/W$ and $g_L-m_L=g_L-1+1/W-S_L$,
\[
\frac1{V_L}=W\Bigl(\frac1W-(1-g_L)-S_L\Bigr)=1-W\bigl[(1-g_L)+S_L\bigr],
\]
which is the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:block}. If $m_L\ge g_L$ this expression is not positive and there is
nothing to prove.

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{(B1)} If the $L-1$ nearest-neighbour bonds of a block are open, the block is good, and each of them is open
with probability $p_1=C$. For the second bound, the block is good if every site of the block except the first has
an open bond to at least one of the sites of the block on its left. For the site with $t$ sites on its left this
has probability $1-\prod_{j=1}^{t}(1-p_j)$, and different sites involve different bonds.

\textbf{(B2)} The function $t\mapsto t^{-1-\sigma}$ is convex, so by Jensen's inequality its average over the $L^2$
pairs $(x,y)$ is at least its value at the average distance. The average of $y-x$ is exactly $rL$. Hence
$D_r\ge L^2\,(rL)^{-1-\sigma}=L^{1-\sigma}r^{-1-\sigma}$.

\textbf{(B3)} Using $1-x\le e^{-x}$ in every factor of \eqref{eq:pL}, $1-p^{(L)}_r\le e^{-C D_r}$. Therefore
\[
\frac{1}{p^{(L)}_r}-1=\frac{1-p^{(L)}_r}{p^{(L)}_r}\le\frac{e^{-CD_r}}{1-e^{-CD_r}}=\frac{1}{e^{CD_r}-1}\le\frac{1}{C\,D_r}.
\]
The first inequality holds because $q/(1-q)$ increases with $q$, and the second because $e^{a}-1\ge a$. The last
inequality of (B3) is (B2).

title: Proof
body_md:
We take Sibuya steps with $\alpha$ in the window \eqref{eq:window}, and write
$A=\alpha^2\zeta(1+2\alpha-\sigma)$ and $W=W(\alpha)$. We bound the two terms in the bracket of \eqref{eq:block}. By
(B1) and Bernoulli's inequality, $C^{L-1}\ge1-(L-1)(1-C)$,
\[
1-g_L\le1-C^{L-1}\le(L-1)(1-C).
\]
By (B3), and then by (S2) as in the proof of corollary~\ref{cor:bound},
\[
\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2\Bigl(\frac{1}{p^{(L)}_r}-1\Bigr)\le\frac{1}{C\,L^{1-\sigma}}\sum_{r\ge1}\pi_\alpha(r)^2\,r^{1+\sigma}
\le\frac{A}{C\,L^{1-\sigma}} .
\]
Let $L\ge2$ be the smallest integer with $L^{1-\sigma}\ge4WA$. For $C\ge\frac12$ the second term is then at most
$2A/L^{1-\sigma}\le1/(2W)$. The first term is less than $1/(2W)$ when $1-C<1/[2W(L-1)]$. For such $C$, which
are indeed at least $\frac12$ because $W\ge1$ and $L\ge2$, the bracket is less than $1/W$, and
theorem~\ref{thm:block} gives $\theta(C)>0$.
